slides.narration: Welcome to the revision of iterative constructs. In this part we meet the three loops of Java: for, while and do while. slides.heading: The four parts of a loop
slides.body_md: A **loop** repeats a statement or block while a condition is true. Every loop has an **initialisation**, a **test**, a **body** and an **update**. Each pass of the body is called an **iteration**.

rows: gives the loop variable its first value

at the end of every pass

visual.alt: Table of the four parts of a loop: initialisation once at the start, the test before each pass, the body in every pass and the update at the end of every pass

slides.narration: A loop repeats a statement or a block while a condition is true. Every loop has four parts. The initialisation gives the loop variable its first value, and it is done once. The test decides whether another pass is made. The body holds the statements that are repeated. The update changes the loop variable at the end of every pass.

slides.narration: The for loop keeps the initialisation, the test and the update together in one header, separated by semicolons. The flowchart shows the order. The initialisation is done once. Then the condition is tested. If it is true the body runs, then the update, and control goes back to the test. If it is false, the loop ends. Because the test comes first, a for loop is entry controlled.

visual.caption: do-while: body first, test afterwards; the body runs at least once.

slides.narration: In the do while loop the body comes first and the test comes afterwards. The flowchart shows that the body is executed, then the condition is tested, and if it is true control returns to the body. Because the test is at the end, the loop is exit controlled. Do not forget the semicolon after the closing bracket of the condition.

slides.heading: Entry-controlled and exit-controlled loops
slides.body_md: The for and while loops are **entry-controlled**: the body may not run at all. The do-while loop is **exit-controlled**: the body runs **at least once**.

rows: `body runs, n = 10 / after the loop, n = 11`

visual.alt: Table showing that with a condition that is false from the start the while loop prints only after the loop, n = 10 while the do-while loop runs its body once and prints body runs, n = 10 / after the loop, n = 11
visual.caption: The only difference is where the test is made.

slides.narration: Here the condition is false from the start. The while loop tests first, finds the condition false, and never runs its body, so only the last line is printed. The do while loop runs its body once before the test, so the body line appears once, and n becomes eleven. This is the one difference between the two kinds of loops.

slides.heading: Counting the passes of a loop
slides.body_md: To count the passes, write down the values of the loop variable that **satisfy the test**. The number of such values is the number of times the body is executed. If the test is false at the start, the number is **0**.

visual.caption: List the values of the variable that pass the test: their number is the number of passes.

slides.narration: To count how often a body runs, list the values of the loop variable that satisfy the test. The number of those values is the number of passes. The table shows four loops, including one that counts down and one whose test is false at the start, so its body never runs. Be careful with the limit: less than and less than or equal to give different counts.

slides.heading: Two counters in one for loop

visual.alt: Trace table of the loop with two counters: the pairs 1 and 10, 3 and 8, 5 and 6 pass the test, and the next pair 7 and 4 fails it
visual.caption: Both counters are initialised and updated together; the commas separate the expressions.

slides.narration: A for loop may have more than one counter. In the header the initialisations are separated by commas, and so are the updates, but there is only one test. In this loop a starts at one and goes up by two, while b starts at ten and goes down by two. The loop continues while a is less than b, and it stops when the pair seven and four fails the test.

slides.heading: Infinite loops

rows: i is never updated, so the test never fails
an empty condition counts as true

visual.alt: Table of four loops that never end, with the reason for each and the way to end it: while true needs a break, a missing update needs an update statement, for with empty parts needs a break, and an empty update part needs an update
visual.caption: These loops are shown, never executed.

slides.narration: An infinite loop never ends by itself. It happens when the condition is always true, when the update statement is missing, or when the for header has empty parts. The table lists four such loops and how to end them: add a break inside an if, or correct the update. A loop written with the condition true and a break, run for four passes, ends with the counter equal to four.

slides.heading: Delay loops and the stray semicolon

rows: `for (int w = 1; w <= 1000000; w++);` between two println statements
empty body: the loop only uses time
i is 6 when the test finally fails

visual.alt: Table of delay loops: a loop with an empty body between two println statements prints Start / Ready; with the variable declared before the loop its final value is 6; a statement after the semicolon runs only once
visual.caption: A semicolon after the header makes the body empty.

slides.narration: A delay loop repeats an empty body many times just to use up time. The semicolon right after the header is the empty body. The first row shows a delay between the words Start and Ready. If the semicolon is put there by mistake, the statement that follows is outside the loop. The second row shows that i is six when the loop ends, and the third shows that a counter statement runs only once.

slides.heading: break: leaving the loop

rows: break: the loop ends at once

visual.alt: Trace table of the break loop: for i from 1 to 4 the test i == 5 is false and i is printed; at i equal to 5 the test is true and break ends the loop, so the output is 1 2 3 4 done

slides.narration: The break statement ends the loop immediately. In this loop, i takes the values one to four and each is printed. When i reaches five, the test is true, break runs, and control jumps to the line after the loop, so the word done is printed. The value five is never printed, and the loop never reaches six, seven or eight.

slides.heading: continue: skipping one pass

rows: skips the rest of this pass only
the update of the for loop, then the test

visual.alt: Table comparing break and continue on the same loop: break prints 1 2 3 4 done and continue prints 1 2 3 4 6 7 8 done

slides.narration: The continue statement skips the rest of the current pass only. In a for loop control goes to the update, and then to the test, so the loop goes on. Compare the two loops. With break, the output stops after four. With continue, only the value five is missing and the loop runs on to eight. This is the difference between break and continue.

visual.alt: Trace table of the loop with continue and break: i 1 is printed; i 2 is printed; i 3 is printed; i 4 is printed; i 5 is continue; i 6 is printed; i 7 is printed; i 8 is break; the printed numbers are 1 2 3 4 6 7

slides.narration: Let us trace a loop that uses both statements. Multiples of five are skipped with continue. When the square of i is above sixty, break ends the loop. For one, two, three and four, the number is printed. Five is skipped. Six and seven are printed. For eight the square is sixty four, so break ends the loop. The printed numbers are one, two, three, four, six and seven.

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: entry and exit-controlled loops, converting between loops, counting passes, infinite and delay loops, and break against continue

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. For and while loops are entry controlled, and the do while loop is exit controlled, with a semicolon after its condition. A for loop can be converted into a while or do while loop by moving the initialisation before the loop and the update into the body. Count passes by listing the values that satisfy the test. Infinite loops never end, delay loops have an empty body, and break leaves a loop while continue skips one pass.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: To count passes or find output, make a trace table: one row for each value of the loop variable, ending with the failing test.
When you convert loops, keep the initialisation, the test and the update; do not forget the semicolon after do-while.
A semicolon right after a for or while header is an empty body: the next statement runs only once.
break leaves the loop; continue skips one pass and the for loop still executes its update.
Never write an infinite loop in an answer unless a break ends it.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. To count passes or find output, make a trace table with one row for each value of the loop variable, and end with the test that fails. When you convert loops, keep the three parts and do not forget the semicolon after a do while. A semicolon right after a loop header is an empty body. Break leaves the loop, and continue skips only one pass. Never leave an infinite loop in an answer unless a break ends it.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. Here we use loops to solve problems. We start by taking a number apart digit by digit. Then we write programs to reverse a number and test for palindrome, prime, perfect and Armstrong numbers, to print a Fibonacci series, and to find the HCF and LCM. After that we study nested for loops, print rectangular and triangular patterns, and find the sum of a series.

slides.heading: Taking a number apart

visual.caption: n % 10 takes the last digit; n / 10 removes it.

slides.narration: To take a number apart, use two operators. The remainder after division by ten is the last digit. Integer division by ten removes the last digit. In the loop for four thousand eight hundred twenty five, the digits come out as five, two, eight and four, and n shrinks until it reaches zero, which ends the loop.

slides.narration: In this program each pass takes the last digit, counts it, adds it to the sum, and removes it from n. For four thousand eight hundred twenty five the digits are five, two, eight and four. The count reaches four and the sum reaches nineteen. The program prints the two results after the loop.

visual.caption: A palindrome equals its reverse.

slides.narration: A palindrome reads the same from both ends. To test one, reverse a copy of the number and compare the reverse with the original. The copy is needed because the loop destroys the number it works on. The table shows that one thousand two hundred twenty one and twelve thousand three hundred twenty one are palindromes, and four thousand five hundred ninety two is not.

slides.heading: Prime numbers

visual.alt: Table of prime tests by counting factors: 13 has 2 factors and prints 13 is prime; 21 has 4 factors and prints 21 is not prime; 29 has 2 factors and prints 29 is prime; 1 has 1 factors and prints 1 is not prime
visual.caption: A prime number has exactly two factors.

slides.narration: A prime number has exactly two factors, one and itself. The program counts the factors of n with a loop from one to n. Thirteen and twenty nine have two factors, so they are prime. Twenty one has four factors, so it is not prime. The number one has only one factor, so it is not prime either.

slides.heading: Perfect numbers

nodes.label: if i divides n: add i to sum

visual.alt: Flow of the perfect-number test: set sum to 0, loop i from 1 to n minus 1, add every i that divides n, then compare sum with n
visual.caption: The number itself is not added.

slides.narration: A perfect number is equal to the sum of its factors other than itself. The flow shows the plan. Start with the sum zero. Loop the counter from one to n minus one, and add every counter value that divides n. At the end compare the sum with n. The number itself is not added, which is why the loop stops one short of n.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: perfect or not?
slides.body_md: Run the perfect-number test for 6, 12 and 28 and list the factors found.

visual.alt: Table of perfect-number tests: 6 has factors 1, 2, 3 with sum 6, so it is perfect; 12 has factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 with sum 16, so it is not perfect; 28 has factors 1, 2, 4, 7, 14 with sum 28, so it is perfect

slides.narration: Let us test three numbers. The factors of six other than six itself are one, two and three, and they add up to six, so six is perfect. For twelve the factors one, two, three, four and six add up to sixteen, which is not twelve, so twelve is not perfect. For twenty eight the factors add up to twenty eight, so twenty eight is perfect.

slides.heading: Armstrong numbers

rows: `123 is not an Armstrong number, sum = 36`

visual.alt: Table of Armstrong tests with cubes: for 153 the cubes 27, 125, 1 give the sum 153, so 153 is an Armstrong number; for 123 the sum is 36, so 123 is not an Armstrong number, sum = 36
visual.caption: The power is the number of digits; here there are three digits.

slides.narration: An Armstrong number equals the sum of its digits, each raised to the power of the number of digits. The program first counts the digits, then adds the powers. The Math dot pow method returns a double, so it must be cast to int. sections.heading: 1. Loops and the for loop
sections.body_md:
A **loop** (iterative construct) repeats a statement or block while a condition is true. Every loop has an **initialisation**, a **test**, a **body** and an **update**; each execution of the body is an **iteration** or pass.

The **for** loop keeps the three control parts in one header:

```java
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    sum += i;
    System.out.println("i = " + i + ", sum = " + sum);
}
```

Output:

```
i = 1, sum = 1
i = 2, sum = 3
i = 3, sum = 6
i = 4, sum = 10
i = 5, sum = 15
```

The initialisation is done once; the test is made before every pass; the update follows the body.

One execution of the body of a loop.
An entry-controlled loop that keeps the initialisation, the test and the update in one header.

**Several counters:** a for header may initialise and update several variables, separated by commas, with one test.

```java
for (int a = 1, b = 10; a < b; a += 2, b -= 2)
    System.out.print(a + "-" + b + " ");
```

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- A semicolon after a for or while header: the body is empty and the next statement runs once.
- Forgetting the semicolon after the condition of a do-while.
- Forgetting the update, which makes the loop infinite.
- Off-by-one errors with < and <= when counting passes.
- Destroying the number while extracting digits and then comparing with the changed value.
- Using 1 / i instead of 1.0 / i, or storing Math.pow in an int without a cast.
- Putting println inside the inner loop of a pattern, or after the outer loop.
- Using the same variable name in the outer and the inner loop.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Output questions: each line in the exact order and format; for a trace, show the values of the variables.
- Error questions: the error named, with the line.
- Programs (15 marks): class and method structure, input, loop logic (limits, update, condition), output, variable description or comments.

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes the purpose of an iterative construct (loop) in Java?

options.text_md: It chooses one block of statements out of several by testing conditions in turn
It repeats a statement or a block of statements as long as its condition stays true
It compares one selector with a list of constant labels and runs the matching case
It stores many values of the same type under a single name

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It repeats a statement or a block of statements as long as its condition stays true. A loop executes its body again and again while the condition holds. Choosing between blocks is the work of if statements and switch, and storing many values under one name is the work of arrays.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following loops tests its condition only after the body has been executed, and is therefore called an exit-controlled loop?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** do-while loop. The do-while loop is the only exit-controlled loop of Java: it runs the body first and tests the condition at the end. The for loop and the while loop are entry-controlled, because they test the condition before every execution of the body.

questions.stem_md: A student says, "The body of a do-while loop is executed at least once, even if its condition is false in the beginning." What is the reason for this?

options.text_md: The condition is placed at the end, so it is tested after the body has already run
The condition is placed before the body, but it is ignored the first time
A do-while loop has no condition and stops only when break is used
The initialisation of the loop variable is written inside the body

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The condition is placed at the end, so it is tested after the body has already run. In a do-while the order is body first, test later. In `int n = 10; do { ... n++; } while (n < 5);` the body runs once and the test n < 5 then fails. A while loop with the same condition would not run its body at all.

**Correct option: (c)** `5`. n takes the values 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25, and the test n < 30 stops the loop at 30, so the body runs 5 times. The count 6 comes from the test n <= 30, 4 from starting at 10, and 7 from starting at 0 with n <= 30.

questions.stem_md: Which part of a loop gives the loop variable its first value, and is executed only once, before the first test?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The initialisation. The initialisation is carried out once, before anything else. The test is made before each pass (after it in do-while), the body is repeated, and the update changes the loop variable at the end of every pass.

**Correct option: (a)** `int k = 10; while (k >= 4) { System.out.print(k + " "); k -= 2; }`. The for loop prints `10 8 6 4`. A while loop needs the initialisation before the loop, the same test, and the update as the last statement of the body. Putting the update first prints `8 6 4 2`, using k > 4 prints `10 8 6`, and counting upwards prints `4 6 8 10`.

**Correct option: (d)** `} while (n <= 3);`. The condition of a do-while is written in brackets after the keyword while, and the statement ends with a semicolon. The compiler reports "';' expected" when the semicolon is missing, "'(' expected" when the brackets are missing, and "while expected" for until, which Java does not have.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The body of a for loop may not be executed even once.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The for loop is entry-controlled, so its condition is tested first. For `for (int i = 9; i < 5; i++)` the test is false at the start, and a counter placed in the body shows 0 executions.
